questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the Watson and Crick structure of DNA. *[10 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
In 1953 **Watson and Crick** proposed the **double helix** model of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), built from X-ray diffraction photographs (Franklin and Wilkins) and from Chargaff's base ratios.

**1. The building block.** DNA is a **polynucleotide**. Each **nucleotide** has three parts: a **pentose sugar (deoxyribose)**, a **phosphate group** and a **nitrogenous base**. The bases are the **purines** (adenine A, guanine G; double ring) and the **pyrimidines** (thymine T, cytosine C; single ring). Nucleotides are joined into a chain by **phosphodiester bonds** between the 3' carbon of one sugar and the phosphate on the 5' carbon of the next, forming a **sugar-phosphate backbone**.

**2. Two strands.** The molecule is made of **two polynucleotide chains** coiled round each other to form a **right-handed double helix**. The two strands are **antiparallel**: one runs 5' to 3' and the other 3' to 5'.

**3. Backbone outside, bases inside.** The sugar-phosphate backbones are on the **outside** and the nitrogenous bases are stacked on the **inside**, at right angles to the long axis of the helix.

**4. Complementary base pairing.** The strands are held together by **hydrogen bonds** between bases: **adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds)** and **guanine pairs with cytosine (three hydrogen bonds)**. A large purine always pairs with a small pyrimidine, so the **width of the helix is constant (about 2 nm)**. The two strands are therefore **complementary**: the sequence of one determines the sequence of the other, and this is the basis of replication. In any DNA, A = T and G = C (Chargaff's rules).

**5. Dimensions.** The bases are **0.34 nm** apart, and there are **10 base pairs per complete turn**, so one turn of the helix measures **3.4 nm**. The helix has a **major groove and a minor groove**.

**6. Information.** The **sequence of bases** along a strand is the genetic code; any order of bases is possible along a strand, which allows an enormous variety of genes.

**Diagram expected.** A labelled drawing of the double helix (two backbones, the 5' and 3' ends of each strand, the base pairs A-T with 2 bonds and G-C with 3 bonds, the distances 0.34 nm, 3.4 nm and 2 nm) and a flat ladder diagram of a short length of the molecule showing deoxyribose, phosphate and the bases.

questions.enonce_markdown: Why is starch molecule a convenient storage form of Carbohydrates in plants? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. Starch is **insoluble in water** and a very large molecule, so it has **no effect on the water potential** of the cell (it does not draw water in by osmosis) and it **cannot diffuse out** of the cell.
2. It is **compact**: amylose is coiled into a helix and amylopectin is branched, so **a large number of glucose units are stored in a small space**.
3. It is **chemically inert** (unreactive), so it does not interfere with cell reactions, and it is **easily hydrolysed by amylase** to maltose and then glucose when energy or building material is needed.

(Any two well explained points earn the 2 marks.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Distinguish between:

(i) Glycogen and Starch.

(ii) Phospholipids and Triglycerides. *[8 marks]* *(10, 2, 8 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Glycogen and starch** (both are polysaccharides made of $\alpha$-glucose units, used as stores)

| Feature | Glycogen | Starch |
|---|---|---|
| Where found | Animals and fungi (stored in liver and muscle cells) | Plants (in chloroplasts and in storage organs such as amyloplasts of tubers and seeds) |
| Composition | One molecule type only: a branched chain of $\alpha$-glucose | A mixture of **amylose** (unbranched, helical, $\alpha$-1,4 bonds) and **amylopectin** (branched, $\alpha$-1,4 and $\alpha$-1,6 bonds) |
| Branching | **Very highly branched** (a branch every 8 to 12 glucose units) | Less branched (amylopectin has a branch every 24 to 30 units; amylose has none) |
| Colour with iodine solution | Red-brown | Blue-black |
| Hydrolysis | More free ends, so it is broken down **faster** (rapid release of glucose) | Slower release |
| Size and solubility | Molecules are large but form fine granules, slightly more soluble | Larger granules, insoluble |

**(ii) Phospholipids and triglycerides** (both are lipids with ester bonds)

| Feature | Phospholipids | Triglycerides |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | **Glycerol + two fatty acids + one phosphate group** (often linked to a small group such as choline) | **Glycerol + three fatty acids** joined by ester bonds |
| Polarity | **Amphipathic**: the phosphate head is **hydrophilic** (polar), the two fatty acid tails are **hydrophobic** | **Entirely hydrophobic** (non-polar) |
| Behaviour in water | Form a **bilayer**, micelles or a monolayer at the surface | Form separate **oil droplets** (emulsion) |
| Main function | Structural: the **basic component of cell membranes** (bilayer) | **Energy store** (about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate), **heat insulation**, protection of organs, buoyancy, source of metabolic water |
| Fatty acids | Often one saturated and one unsaturated | Saturated (fats) or unsaturated (oils) |
